Orwell is a really cool idea. You take the role as a investigator tasked with combing thru internet records and conversations of members of an activist group to find out if any of them are the culprit in a terrorist bombing. It's a slow game, but engageing. Also shouldn't surpise anyone that's it is a really political game, a scathing comment on totalitarian survailence.  

The gameplay concists of finding importatnt information and uploading them to your supervisor. The clever part with the mechanics is that you can choose to upload or not upload various data and while it at first seems like you really have no control over how the information will be used, that's kind of the point of the game. Depending on what you choose to upload pretty much everyone can be made look guilty, be it from off hand comments, things taken out of context or carefully selected data while ignoring other information. Yeah, did I mention that it's kind of obvious what the devs think of the concept of Big Brother... The dialogues and plot are very well writen and is belivable for the most part. The ending is kind of brilliant. 

The only thing I think they could have done better with was that they made the nation and political party in power in the game kind of fascist to begin with, it would have been a lot more clever to have it take place in a country that was much less a police state and still have the orwell system in place. But overall a really good and unique game.

In Conclusion, 

Orwell is a reasonably thrilling game about being a cog in a surveillance state. It requires a substantial amount of reading, with many insignificant choices, and only a few consequential decisions. It makes reasonable use of a unique visual aesthetic, and good musical cues, but is hampered by only average dialogue between the characters. The story moves along swiftly enough, as long as one isn't too picky about what they pass along to Symes, especially because progressing requires submitting most of the data available. Orwell doesn't have much unique that hasn't already been said about surveillance, but the ending is reasonably powerful and compelling.

I enjoyed Orwell a bit , but it's not as much a superior offspring from 1984, as a subordinate clause.

[h1]Orwell - Parts 1 and 2[/h1]

[b]Orwell[/b] was a fairly unique experience, with perhaps some similarities to visual novels and point-and-click puzzle games. It is well made and combines narrative and gameplay to keep the player intrigued and eager to find out more. It also seems to have plenty of replay value with a number of different paths and outcomes available depending on the choices you make. Whilst the same can be said of Orwell: Ignorance is Strength it doesn’t quite pack the same punch. The second instalment is shorter, has less variety in terms of proceedings and outcomes and the narrative is not as well written or constructed.

In short, if you’re looking for a slow-paced, thought-provoking game with a political theme (and don’t mind 4-6 hours of reading) I’d definitely recommend Orwell but maybe give Orwell: Ignorance is Strength a miss, or approach it with lower expectations.

For a full comparative review of both installments of Orwell, click [url=https://indie-hive.com/orwell-comparative-review/] here [/url]

[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

I don't review games very often, but I felt that I needed to throw out my two cents on this game. I haven't read any other reviews, so I'm not influenced by what other people think of it.

I went into this game almost entirely blind. I got it a long while ago, and just got around to installing and playing it today. I sat down to give it a quick try, see if I would enjoy it, and ... 3 hours later, I finished the story. It's not a sprawling 100 hour experience, but those 3 hours were intense, and I was locked into the events the entire time.

A brief summary: you play an Investigator using a program called Orwell, which sifts through social media profiles and newspaper articles (and maybe listens in on a few phone calls) to try to track down criminals. Specifically, a bomb has gone off in a public plaza, and you need to find out who did it.

There are some great twists and turns along the way, and I enjoyed myself the entire time. One moment in particular had me literally on the edge of my seat, biting my lip while I listened to a conversation unfold, unable to do anything but wait to see what would happen. This was a conversation that only occurred because of choices that I had made, and in the end, I had to live with the consequences of those choices. It was rough, and it was emotional, but it was amazing.

Anyway, I love this game. I give it a 4/5 on my "arbitrary 5 point rating scale". The writing felt a little clunky at times, which is really the only complaint that I have, and it's not bad enough to really detract from the experience. Please give this game a try!

Graphics: 5/5
 - It's VERY stylized, so it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but I really loved the way everything looked. The UI was clean and easy to maneuver, and the portraits and pictrues were very compelling for me.

Sound: 4.5/5
 - Very immersive music, and the sound effects felt right at home. Since there's no audible dialogue in this game (when you're "listening" to a phone conversation, you're reading the text transcription of that conversation), the music rising and falling gave some amazing feels. There are also times that the music will suddenly move from calm and serene the intense and pounding when you're reading articles or some such, indication that you've found a piece of information that drastically changes things. I give it 4.5 instead of 5 because the different tracks don't flow into each other - when one starts, the previous one stops instantly, giving a weird stutter.

Gameplay: 4.5/5
 - The gameplay is very simple: click, drag, scroll, read. There's no much to it, and for the most part, everything is very responsive. The .5 points left off was for the fact that, occasionally, dragging data into place was a pain in the ass. Sometimes my pointer just wouldn't grab ahold of something.

Writing: 4/5
 - The story itself is awesome and very compelling. Often times, the dialogue was fine, but there were some times that the dialogue felt stilted and clunky, and unnatural, sounding like someone writing lines for a game, rather than natural conversation. Again, it didn't affect my enjoyment, but it was something I noticed.

Replayability: 3/5
 - Here's the thing. I haven't played the game a second time yet, but it's definitely possible to do so. There are events within the game that would have gone differently if I'd chosen different options (I won't forgive myself for failing to prevent an attack). The reason I say 3/5 is because there would still be a LOT of repetition to sit through. Many conversations that you will already know the outcome of, that move along at the same pace as before. That pace is AWESOME when you're reading everything for the first time, but on a second playthrough, it will probably get tedious. Once I play through a second time, I will readdress this score, but for now, the 3/5 represents the fact that I don't really want to play through a second time for a while.

Use Orwell to dig through suspect's web history and social media, spy on e-mails and texts as they're sent, and listen-in on phone conversations. With the information you compile, hopefully you are able to stop the next terrorist attack before it happens... or perhaps you will uncover the dark, looming purpose of Orwell.

In a time when the topic of surveillance vs. privacy is ever more discussed, Orwell gives a lot to think about. Great story, good character representation; expect to find yourself on the edge of your seat. Only wish that it was a bit longer.

I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

I honestly didn't think this game would absorb me as much as it did.

Orwell is basically a distopian novel played out in the role of an government investigator that's tracking who's behind "The Nation" security, watching out for terrorist activities. You gather information, listen to conversations, spy on devices and find incriminating evidence.

I think the social commentary that the game creates surrounding the use of technology and social media as a gateway to keep track of every single citizen and how easy it is to either be tracked or be impersonated is amazing. We really don't have a great concept of just how much info we voluntarily give to the web, how every single action that we do remains like an unerasable stain floating in the net.

The gameplay is pretty bland, but despite that, I just couldn't get my mind out from the story. It's engaging, entangling, immersive and so well written that I just kept on going and going and going. There's A HUGE LOT of reading to do that's for sure, but it's made in a way that incites the player to keep reading, to uncover every single truth out there, behind the ever-looking eye of the "Big Brother"

I absolutely loved how this also turns around the whole concept of George Orwell's 1984 in a modernized, updated and completely realistic setting. We don't have to keep on imagining and wondering how a society under eternal surveillance looks like. We are already living it.

Aside from some issues where relevant information wasn't "flagged" for selection, and the occasional goofy conversation, Orwell is a pretty solid game about the pitfalls of the surveillance state. You witness the story unfolding through articles, conversations, and eventually some more intrusive searching, and have the opportunity to decide what is and is not worthy of consideration. In doing so you change the course of the investigation itself, casting suspicion based on your reporting to your advisor.

It's executed pretty well, with a good style and simple interface. It starts off fairly straightforward, and you're left to discover for yourself just how subjective the process can be. You'll be railroaded a bit into reporting certain information for the story to proceed, but there's plenty of wiggle room for you to be the by-the-book investigator or the secret resistance hero with what you do and do not upload.

Not sure if I want to go back through and try to influence the story more heavily than my first play through, but it's made me very interested in the second season.

Goodness, when was the last time I one-shotted a game? Just finished Orwell, having only taken a break for supper, and boy what a game. Bravo to everyone involved.

I think the game first of all deserves plaudits for style and storytelling, interwoven into gameplay. This kind of indie game really shows what's capable in interactive media, including making the player a participant in the activities. No two ways about it, you don't walk away with clean hands from this narritive. And god, that's just unbelievably cool. I can't think of any other medium that works as well. By uncovering the stories that these characters contain, the player gets pulled into the drama and hell, I'd say I believe these characters more than I would in a traditional triple-A game narritive. This is partially due to the strength of the writing but also due to the computer interface framing device which allows for a completely seamless experience.

But what this game really does well is play with its themes. It's a power trip, to dig through people's lives and find the bits and pieces that fit into a story that you can tell someone else. It's also remarkably disturbing how plausible it all is, and how effectively the player can go about their business. As I played, I started wondering to myself how much art might imitate life. How far away are we from the very horror portrayed here? How do we defeat such a tool? Is there anywhere else to go after that?

The game also does a great job of leaving a very plausible trail of breadcrumbs to follow, with a good amount of leeway into what needs to be found and in what order. The actual layout of the story isn't entirely known to me (what exactly is cleverly scripted) but I'd say the rails are actually fairly wide at parts, and usually coming to a head with each chapter. The space to move around here is necessary both to keep the player engaged and addicted, but also to make the simulation seem plausible. If the story was too narrow it would feel a bit too pre-arranged, but there's some actual detective work to do here and that's quite marvelous, if not novel.

For those on the fence, play this game. Completely worth your 5 hours. With a chaser of Citizenfour while you're at it. Crazy that I'm playing with the notion of a game properly adding to the political discourse, yet here we are. I suspect this game will linger with me for a long while.
